body.objective: Students will be able to name foods and drinks.
body.iCan: I can name foods and drinks.
successCriteria: I can name common foods and drinks in French
I can say what I eat at each meal
I can say what I like to eat and drink
body.hook: Croissants, poutine, tourtière, crêpes: French-speaking cultures have given the world some famous foods. Learning food vocabulary is also learning about culture.

study.title: Bon appétit !
study.question: What foods and drinks do I eat in a day?
study.passage:
Text (read aloud):
Au petit-déjeuner, je mange des céréales et une banane. Je bois du lait.
Au dîner, à l'école, je mange un sandwich au poulet et une pomme. Je bois de l'eau.
Au souper, avec ma famille, nous mangeons du riz, du poisson et des légumes.
Le week-end, mon père prépare des crêpes. Miam !
Food culture: poutine (fries, cheese curds and gravy) comes from Quebec; tourtière is a meat pie eaten at holidays in Quebec; crêpes are thin pancakes from France.
Verbs: manger (je mange, tu manges, il mange, nous mangeons); boire (je bois, tu bois, il boit).
Activity: sort food pictures into breakfast, lunch and supper; then ask a partner: Qu'est-ce que tu manges au petit-déjeuner ?
study.source: Original text written for this lesson.
discussion: What does the writer eat for breakfast?
What do you eat for supper?
How are mealtime words in Canada different from France?
study.product: Describe what you eat and drink at each meal in a short paragraph, using manger and boire.

body.objective: Students will be able to use du, de la and des.
body.iCan: I can use du, de la and des.
successCriteria: I can use du, de la, de l' and des for "some"
I can use de after negatives and quantities
I can describe a meal with correct articles
body.hook: In English we say "I eat bread" or "some bread." In French you can't leave the article out: je mange du pain. These little words (du, de la, des) are called partitive articles, and they're used every time you talk about food.

study.title: Du, de la, des
study.question: How do I say "some" in French?
study.passage:
Partitive guide (written for this lesson):
Use partitives for an unknown amount of something:
Masculine: du (du fromage, du poulet). Feminine: de la (de la soupe, de la tarte). Before a vowel: de l' (de l'eau, de l'ananas). Plural: des (des pommes, des légumes).
After a negative, all become de (d' before a vowel): Je ne mange pas de viande. Je ne bois pas d'eau gazeuse.
After quantities, use de: beaucoup de fromage, un peu de sucre, une bouteille d'eau, un kilo de pommes.
But after aimer, adorer, détester (general likes), use le/la/les: J'aime le fromage (cheese in general).
Activity: "Le pique-nique": groups plan a picnic basket and write sentences: Dans le panier, il y a du pain, de la limonade, des fraises… Then a partner asks Est-ce qu'il y a du chocolat ? → Non, il n'y a pas de chocolat.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

Plan a picnic basket in French

body.objective: Students will be able to order politely in a café.
body.iCan: I can order politely in a café.
successCriteria: I can order politely in a café using je voudrais
I can ask for prices and the bill
I can role-play a café conversation
body.hook: Walk into a café in Quebec City, Moncton or Paris and you'll hear "Bonjour, je voudrais…" over and over. Ordering politely is one of the most practical skills a French learner can have.

study.title: Au café
study.question: How do I order politely in a café?
study.passage:
Dialogue (read in threes):
Serveur : Bonjour ! Vous désirez ?
Amira : Bonjour ! Je voudrais un chocolat chaud et un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
Serveur : Et pour vous ?
Ben : Je voudrais un jus d'orange et une crêpe au sucre, s'il vous plaît.
Serveur : Et avec ça ?
Ben : C'est tout, merci.
(plus tard)
Amira : L'addition, s'il vous plaît. C'est combien ?
Serveur : Ça fait treize dollars cinquante.
Amira : Voilà. Merci, au revoir !
Café menu (in dollars): chocolat chaud 3,50 $; café au lait 3,75 $; jus d'orange 3,00 $; croissant 2,75 $; crêpe au sucre 4,25 $; sandwich jambon-fromage 7,50 $.
Note: French writes decimals with a comma (3,50) and in Canada the $ often comes after the number.
Politeness: use vous with servers; always start with Bonjour.
Activity: role-play in threes with the menu; the server totals the bill.
study.source: Original dialogue and menu written for this lesson.
discussion: Why does the server say vous?
How is 3,50 $ written differently from English?
What did your group's bill total?
study.product: Perform a café role-play using at least six polite phrases, and write the order and total bill in French.
